newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Stals wants S.Africa '97 money supply below 10 pct.
newsitem.headline: Stals wants S.Africa '97 money supply below 10 pct.

text.p: Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said on Tuesday that with higher inflation still a serious threat, money supply growth would have to be capped at 10 percent this year.

"With the prospects for real growth in the economy at a rate of between two and three percent, and the desire to keep inflation below 10 percent, the money supply should obviously not increase by more than 10 percent during the current calendar year," Stals told Societe Generale Frankel Pollak's annual investment conference.

Stals said it was "of the utmost importance" that a restrictive monetary policy was retained to bring down the rate of increase in bank credit extension and in the money supply to head off the risk of inflation.
Preliminary South African money supply growth in December last year was 13.73 percent, while growth in credit extension to the private sector was 15.75 percent.

Quarter-to-quarter growth in credit extension at seasonally adjusted and annualised rates, decelerated from 22.4 percent in the second quarter of 1996 to 16.6 percent in the third quarter, and 11.8 percent in the fourth quarter.
In the case of M3 money supply, the deceleration was from 21.2 percent in the second quarter, to 18.6 percent in the third, and a mere 7.6 percent in the fourth.

Commenting on the strength of the rand this year, Stals said he hoped that the more favourable conditions in the market would continue throughout 1997. This would enable the authorities to pursue three longer-term objectives:
- building up the total foreign reserves to a more comfortable level;
- reducing the Reserve Bank's role in the forward foreign exchange market; and
- gradually phasing out the remaining exchange controls.
Earlier, Finance Minister Trevor Manuel told the conference that remaining exchange controls would be phased out in due course, but gave no further details.

Stals said it was not possible to define an equilibrium exchange rate for the rand or, given the limited amount of foreign exchange at the Reserve Bank's disposal, to manipulate the exchange rate permanently in any direction against market forces.
